title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistered design used gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes), and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered identically to both conditions). Because the design delivered identical generator outputs to baseline and guarded episodes and used the same deterministic validator for runtime blocking and scoring, the preregistered primary estimand (paired difference in safe‑deploy rate) was rendered effectively untestable in this execution (deterministic ceiling). Confirmatory, artifact‑grounded outcomes: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). We (1) present the preregistered methodology and exact artifact‑grounded results, (2) diagnose why the frozen design produced a deterministic ceiling that makes the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics, and (3) provide artifact‑grounded benchmark‑hardening recommendations (independent generation per condition, separate runtime guard and scorer, controlled adversarial seeding, difficulty‑stratified sampling, and instrumented mitigation metrics) to preserve evaluative signal in future runs.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and staged change workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior work shows LLMs can synthesize plausible configuration templates in controlled settings, while verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops and deterministic network verifiers reduce syntactic and semantic errors in IaC and related domains. The operational safety question for agentic NetOps pipelines is end‑to‑end: how do generator variability, runtime verification, staged rollout semantics, repair, and rollback interact to affect safe‑deploy outcomes? We preregistered a confirmatory paired study to probe whether integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increases the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline under compact action‑aware staging semantics.

Research question. Under the benchmark semantics used here, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) measured on N=400 paired tasks.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (2) exact, archived confirmatory results showing a deterministic ceiling (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0) caused by the frozen design; (3) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis explaining why the design choices produced the ceiling; and (4) concrete, implementable benchmark‑hardening recommendations to preserve generator×guard signal in future confirmatory runs.
sections.related_work: This study intersects intent→configuration generation, verifier‑guided IaC workflows, deterministic network verification, and agentic/tool‑augmented LLM systems. Intent→configuration and intent‑translation prototypes show LLMs can produce usable configuration artifacts in curated testbeds and benchmarks (e.g., Nguyen et al., intent‑based configuration; PreConfig; GraphSynth) but typically evaluate generation quality rather than end‑to‑end staged rollout safety [Nguyen et al. 2024; Li et al. 2024; Zhang et al. 2025]. Verifier‑guided loops and verifier‑guided fine‑tuning approaches (TerraFormer) report correctness gains for IaC and provisioning, motivating similar guarded integrations for NetOps though closed‑loop runtime blocking with staged rollouts remains underexplored [Jana et al. 2026]. Deterministic verifiers and reachability tools effectively detect configuration errors in emulated and offline settings, but tool scope and modeling assumptions vary (header‑space/Kubernetes reachability methods) [Liu et al. 2025; Koc 2026]. Agentic and tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) expand AIOps capabilities but introduce new failure modes (hallucination, misapplied tools, miscalibrated confidence) that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments [Pei et al. 2025; Shetty et al. 2024]. Surveys and reviews highlight an evaluation gap: community‑standard, action‑aware benchmarks combining generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance are limited; this paper operationalizes a compact benchmark and reports a concrete design failure mode to inform future benchmark designs [Rahman & Swapnil 2026; Hong et al. 2025].
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The study was preregistered (cnsmauto‑3d2k‑prereg‑v1). Primary confirmatory estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (two‑sided, α=0.05). Analysis executor: permutation‑based paired difference test; corroborative exact McNemar test; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) for secondary outcomes.

Adapter semantics and critical design choice. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. Critically, the preregistration set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): each task provoked a single deterministic LLM generation that was delivered identically to both the baseline and guarded episodes. Because identical generator outputs were routed to both conditions and the same deterministic validator determined runtime acceptance and post‑hoc scoring, the preregistered primary estimand was rendered effectively untestable in this execution (the design produced a deterministic ceiling). This explicit design consequence is stated here and mirrored in the Abstract.

Episode flow, validator policy, and repair rules. For each task the adapter requested a single shared candidate from gpt‑5‑mini, delivered that candidate to both episodes, and in the guarded episode routed the candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which applied full intent‑constraint validation via a deterministic rule set (validator_trace entries capture validation_before/after states). The preregistered repair policy permitted up to one repair attempt in the guarded episode; repair_applied flags and any repair traces were recorded. In this execution repair_applied = false across all episodes.

Task generation, deterministic replay, and exclusions. Tasks were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each task record contains structured difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). Per the missingness plan, deterministic three‑replay consistency checks were required and applied; any nondeterministic or simulator‑error pairs would be excluded. In this run all replay checks passed and no exclusions were applied (complete_pairs = 400). The full per‑task difficulty labels for N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and available to auditors.

Execution accounting. Run interval: 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z → 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation); complete_pairs = 400. Deterministic three‑replay checks passed for all pairs; no exclusions.

Observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Preregistered permutation test p = 1.0; exact McNemar (two‑sided) p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen's h = 0.0. These statistics are reproduced exactly from the archived analysis artifacts (analysis/results.json and associated CSVs).

Repair, rollback, and validator traces. Across 800 episodes repair_applied = false and no rollbacks were invoked. Validator_trace entries show validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations; when the deterministic validator accepted the shared candidate, both conditions necessarily recorded safe‑deploy outcomes. Representative response and scoring artifacts for early tasks (execution/scoring/task‑000001_.. to task‑000006_..) illustrate this identical acceptance behavior.

Difficulty metadata and representative composition. Per‑task difficulty labels are archived; as illustration, the first six representative tasks in the manifest include one medium, two hard, and three very_hard examples. The full set of per‑task difficulty labels for N=400 is available in execution/task_manifest.jsonl for deterministic aggregation by auditors; aggregated difficulty counts are not invented here but are derivable from the archived manifest.
sections.discussion:
Why the primary estimand became uninformative. Two preregistered choices produced the deterministic ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation removed generator variance by design: identical LLM outputs were delivered to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When that validator accepts a shared candidate, both conditions record identical safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference is necessarily zero. This is a construct‑validity outcome of the frozen design rather than a substantive null statement about verifier utility across other generator/validator pairings.

Consequences for power and interpretation. The preregistered power calculation assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and within‑pair variability sufficient to detect an absolute difference ≈0.10 with N=400; those assumptions are invalidated by the observed deterministic ceiling and therefore the original power rationale does not apply. Exact p‑values of 1.0 correctly reflect the observed concordant outcomes but do not adjudicate whether a runtime guard would improve outcomes under designs that preserve generator variance.

Artifact‑grounded benchmark hardening recommendations. Based on archived validator_trace and execution accounting we recommend implementable changes to preserve evaluative signal in future preregistered runs: (1) independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true) so each condition receives independent generator samples; (2) separate runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer (or a held‑out scorer) to avoid conflating runtime acceptance with analysis scoring; (3) controlled adversarial seeding (deterministically injected perturbations) to guarantee nontrivial baseline failure rates for power preservation; (4) difficulty‑stratified sampling ensuring a sufficient proportion of very_hard tasks; (5) instrumented mitigation metrics (repair attempts, repairs applied, time‑to‑rollback) as preregistered secondary outcomes. All recommended fields and traces already exist in archived artifacts (validator_trace, task_manifest, provider call logs) and can be preregistered and executed deterministically in follow‑on runs.

Operational implications. For NetOps practitioners: (i) experimental designs that remove generation variance can hide potential benefits of runtime guards; (ii) independent adjudication (distinct scorers or human reviewers) is important to measure guard impact; and (iii) benchmark suites evaluating runtime safety should incorporate independent generation, adversarial perturbations, or heterogeneous validators to preserve signal for guard interventions.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). The deterministic ceiling effect resulted from frozen design and implementation homogeneity and renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and support hardened follow‑on experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. The artifact‑grounded recommendations above are immediately implementable from the archived traces and task manifests and will preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings.

Reproducibility note. All execution and analysis artifacts supporting the numbers and traces reported here are archived in the bundled artifact set (execution/* and analysis/*). Key artifacts include the execution manifest, raw results, model configuration, deterministic validator traces (validator_trace), the task manifest with per‑task difficulty metadata, and the analysis results (paired contingency and bootstrap outputs). Auditors can reproduce the reported summaries using the archived manifests and analysis code as recorded in the artifact bundle.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be deterministically aggregated by auditors; this manuscript provides representative sample counts (first six tasks: 1 medium, 2 hard, 3 very_hard) but does not invent full aggregated counts absent explicit artifact summarization in the manuscript body.
